title: Strategies to increase routine symptom measurement in outpatient depression care: a systematic review
subtitle: Which strategies raise clinician-reviewed measure use, and does higher use change outcomes
statement: Routine symptom measurement is policy in the service's six outpatient clinics, but only 34 percent of depression visits in 2025 had a completed measure, and the executive must choose between an electronic prompt, clinician training with feedback, or no new investment. A systematic review of strategies to increase clinician-reviewed measure use in outpatient depression care, and of whether higher use changes patient outcomes, would inform that choice.
whoAffected: Adults treated for depression in outpatient clinics, their clinicians, and the executive that funds service changes.
whatHurts: When measures are not completed or not looked at, treatment is not adjusted when patients fail to improve, and patients experience the questionnaire as paperwork.
currentPractice: Clinicians are asked to use the PHQ-9 at every visit; use varies from always to never, with no prompt and no feedback.
whyNow: A purchase decision on an electronic prompt is pending, and published strategies differ in cost and durability.
constraints: Two part-time reviewers with about 60 hours each before June 2027, if the second reviewer is released. English and French reports only; no translation budget. No funding for software beyond what the service already licenses.
patientCenteredGoal: Patients' symptom scores are used with them to adjust treatment, so fewer people stay on treatment that is not working.
summary: Problem framed as a systematic review of strategies to raise clinician-reviewed measure use and its effect on outcomes.
